sentences.text: Andrew, how you doing?
This meeting is being recorded.
Very well.
Can you see me?
Yep, I can.
I can't see me at all, but that's fine.
That's no problem.
Might be a good thing.
No, I'm joking.
I don't know why you wouldn't be able to see yourself.
You should be able to if you're looking at the zoom window.
Can you see me?
Yes, I can.
And on the right hand side, it's note taking.
I can see all three of us, the note taker as well as.
Okay, that's all right.
No worries.
That's no problem.
I can see me now.
Yeah.
Maybe I've got control of a spotlight and.
Yes.
Is that right?
Yeah.
Great.
Thank you.
Great.
Well, thanks.
Thanks for, for giving me an hour of your time that I bought as usual.
It's not something I've done before, so I've certainly met with consultants, but I haven't bought someone's time as a commodity over the airwaves.
So I'm looking forward to a rich exchange over the next hour.
Yeah, good.
Well, thank you for booking yourself in and hopefully you've done it on purpose and it's not the only way.
It was like trying to book an appointment with me and it was the only one you could see.
No, there was purpose behind it.
Okay, cool.
All right.
Do you remember that we met at your house?
I think your Airbnb.
That would have been a long time ago.
It would have been, yeah.
About two years ago.
Three years ago.
Badminton.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Well, lots happened in the meantime, but we'll get into that after because I don't want to run, run the clock down.

So, yeah, these sessions really, I sometimes call them tear downs when, when I talk about them on my mailing list because really what I want to do, what I normally want to do is just hear as much about the business as possible and then I, I can kind of give you the low hanging fruit that either possibly you can't see for yourself.
So that, that's kind of the, the usual structure.
But I do see that you've, you've put a bunch of questions in as well.
So I'm happy to stick to your agenda equally if, if that's what you would prefer.
Okay.
Well, I mean, those are the pointers really.
Rather than looking backwards, I want to look forward.
And I don't want to burn an hour talking too much about the business historical and problems or challenges.
But it's about where I'm at now in the future and kind of, you know, I am master and commander of my own destiny at the moment.
And I want to be more creative with the outcomes that.

That happen in the future by exploring through consultations with people like yourselves, you know, at least looking at different potential avenues for accelerating the company and improving the ultimate outcome for all the shareholders.
You know, I put in my note to you that the sort of.
The basic response is, is to, you know, course correct.

You know, adjust to what you see in front of you, make adaptions and remain, you know, a proactive business leader that reads the market and evolves the proposition and refreshes the company and brings new talent in.
You know, that's the kind of day job of running an agency and fishing where the fish are and learning.
But, you know, this is a very fickle industry with lots of external factors influencing, you know, revenues and activity and markets and net figures.
It's also a business utterly dependent on talent.
And the talent can.
Can often not be quite what it says on the tin.
And I have tried.
My snapshot to you is I've.
I look back over 32 years and I've done 250 million in billings with Blue Marlin.
I've had, you know, 15 studios on five continents.
I've had 350 clients and over 1500 staff.
I've had birth deaths.
I've had marriages and affairs.
I've had children, not all my own.
And there's been, you know, a very colorful journey of life.
And in.
In that, in that period of time, the business got to nearly 10 million in revenues in one year.
And we got two sort of serious attempts to bias in that time.
But we're a very different business today.
And so the business now is tiny.
It's a creative boutique.
And in fact, it's been going dark for the last 18 months as we've been focusing on sorting out some problems, but also working out what we want to do.
And our future, I believe, is in recognizing if we do nothing but just stay as we are.
It's evolving to Blue Marlin 6.0 and Blue Marlin 6.0.
If.
If I can share my screen with you?
Yeah, sure.
Let me just make sure you got the.
One sec.
There we go.
So how do I share screen now?
Do I go to more?
Yeah.
Okay.
So you can see my screen and my presentation if I go to full screen.
No, that's not right.
Yeah, I've got.
I've got the full screen.
Okay, cool.

So, yeah, very quickly, I mean, we're talking about evolving the company with a masthead called Blue Marlin, but with two propositions and one is bluespace, which is all about essentially utilizing the strategic and creative minds of not just people here, but people who are on the bench and available for hire as strategic creative mercenaries to do really provocative and different things.

And that's about coming at businesses with imagination and courage, using the currency of creativity, design to solve, but being more open to what we address and therefore being more entrepreneurial as a business.
So stepping into more about the business challenge rather than the medium of delivery being.
It has to be a design project, it could be digital, it could be cultural.
And by doing so we think and we are already selling very valuable time to some key clients that are around things of brand or innovation or culture or experiential.
And these are things that Blue Marlin is not well known for.
Its legacy is in consumer good packaging, 2D and 3D sustainability.
It then means that we're now stepping out of consumable companies and we're getting into airlines and agri and finance of pharma and we are getting into B2B and B2C.

So BlueSpace is the consulting arm of Blue Marlin and Blue Marlin is the realization arm of BlueSpace in terms of the downstream activation of the business and whether we use a sort of conventional process of immersion, discovery outside world influences the client's world and environment, the consumer customer world, and distilling those insights into revelations and then finding brand solutions or project solutions or innovation solutions that ultimately leads to a converged diverge model which then reaches to market.
And you know, clients expect you to be able to do this type of work through all the touch points of the brand world.
And whether we do it internally or through third parties, we're effectively a full service international agency.
Not carrying the cost but aligning the people to the business when we have the business signed.
So we are now a much more smaller business of 12 permanent staff.
We have about six permanent contractors or about 18 people every month, plus some additional freelancers when we need them.
And we're spread out through the us, the UK by geography but not market.
So the UK covers Europe and the GCC region and it does all the creative for India.
And I'll talk you through some details in a minute.
But the people in the business have all been partners in their own companies.
So Y Projects is run by Nick Sunderland, but last year I gave him quarter of a million of fees for work doing for my other clients and creative work.
Andrew McLean runs his own little agency.
He's an AI guy, he's ex head of strategy at an agency, PhD and also bulletproof.
And his brother works at sort of Amazon, I think, as head of AI and so he's a great guy to have as sort of chief technology officer.
Michael's in upstate New York.
He's my lead strategist on John Deere in the United States.
He's ex sterling and interbrand and future brand.
He's a smart guy.
Andrew Mulholland runs his own consulting business in London.
He helps me out on some projects.
Dee's an airline consultant in Miami.
Kim's the creative director in New York.
Sam works for me in London.
Lucia runs her own semiotic company.
So the type of work the Blue Marlin is now doing is quite different.
It's from airlines through to this is a payroll, an HR platform for TMF Group.
And we're making film animations.
You've got a new agribusiness identity in India for a super group there.
So this is new corporate identity that's rolling out across India.
Politics is a new 21st century wound tech product innovation that's done by Polaroid Therapeutics using their film technology.
But getting into wound care, so very diverse.
And you know, John Deere is strategy, it's positioning, it's working with the after parts business.
It's looking at what we do with lubricants and coolants and things.
And it does lead to some packaging, but it leads to lots of other things.
We partnered with Landor in Spain to rebrand Sepsa and Moeve.
And Moeve is the new future business for the Spanish Sepsa business owned by the, the Emiratis.
But this is new structural packaging.
We've done industrial design and it goes on sort of European work for Colgate and in Asia, we're just launching right now a Maltese soft drink right across the world, Kinney.
And we, we've done a lot of positioning work in films and movies and content.
Social CISC is the national beer of Malta.
Rebranding that and then the whole portfolio lean to innovation and, you know, we got some great results.
Sales are up, you know, market leader sales are up 36%.
So entering effectiveness awards and it gives you a sense and then of course moving really to the number of things through some British brands and European brands.
What, what sets us apart at the moment from doing this sort of consumer and comms work is we've actually developed since 2014 a very strong foothold in India and India grew 60% for us last year.
It's now a 1.2 million annual revenues.
It's going to be 1.6 this year.
We're doing stunning work over there, helping national companies develop strong national brands and fight international competition.
And, and they could be working, you know, like creating a new brand here for a company called ITC and Wellness.
You know, they're like a unilever in India and this is Prana, which is their wellness and spirituality brand.
And we're doing assets for, for them.
We're making movies and animations.
So we use this outsource to a production house to make this animal.
And then Darbo is another sort of what I would call tier 2 multinational.
Doing a lot of work for them in consumer goods.
But they have lots of brands in hair care, in personal care, doing work with ITC in three divisions, some well known brands, some less well known.
But it's the wild west out there and we're loving it.
But it comes with its challenges that the more work we do, the more almost in some ways that the less work we're bringing home.
Because the Indian withholding tax is quite strong.
It's at 85 pence in the pound is what we retrieve.
They're holding on to 15 pence.

And one of my notes to you with that introduction was that I've got this withholding tax asset building up on my balance sheet which I can only redeem and bring home and unwind if I'm making excessive UK profits and can offset corporation tax in the UK against the withholding tax that's in India.
Well, that sum is going to pass nearly a million pounds this year and that's a million pounds of net net profits.
So that is going to take me years to unwind that position.
And of course my accountants are telling me, really, you're never going to do it, Andrew, we need to write it down, we need to write it off and therefore depreciate the value of your company.
And I'm saying, hold on a minute guys.

I think I can find someone who's strategically motivated that might a want to buy Blue Marlin to get our access to India, the world's fastest growing consumer economy, get access to our clients, to have our brand power and to give themselves a platform to enter the market and extend their services or our services into the Indian market to get more business and grow that fast.
Second thing is, there might be someone actually who is interested in that.

But additionally is one of these different types of media marketing agencies, comms agencies, that's making really big profits and could see an opportunity here of unwinding that position and Getting the benefit of buying our business gives them a million pounds tax credit.
So those are two things that particularly are relevant to India.
But the thing that really caught my eye recently, I mean though, that's what's been preoccupying my mind.

What do I do with India, given I'm expecting it to continue to grow and that problem to get bigger and bigger and how do I fight off my, my, my uncourageous and unimaginative accountants who are trying to tell me to write down the value of my business and could I do it by finding a strategically motivated partner who can see the opportunity in India and can see the opportunity to use that tax.
The.

The other thing is your communication recently has been about, you know, reach out to me to help, whether it's to give you a health check, whether it's to roll up, whether it's to work with you on an exit, whatever.
Well, I'm 62, you know, I think 65, 67 would be a nice age to wind up.
So I need to get my business in shape.
Three to five years.
I still full of mojo and juice, but I know what I need to do, which is to bring a succession team in.

So I'm actively recruiting for a leadership team in London right now, making decisions on reducing property portfolio, investing in the right areas, but wanting to keep our business tight and small, but better led with better talent.
I want to drive up the.
Financial.
Performance of the business and the KPIs and I can, I can think there's some ways of doing that.
There is a.

One thing that would make a very big difference to the next 12 months is that last year we bid for and won the creation of a new airline, which I just flashed up some of that detail to you on the show Aspire.
We won the bid against the odds of future brand into Brandon Landor by putting together a dream team.
The client though, couldn't move forward because the 380 million of private equity that was coming in to back it from California and Mexico did a runner when Trump, Trump did his tariff wall.
So that funding has been held and postponed for six to nine months.
And it was going to be a $4 million piece of business for me in 12 months getting this airline off the ground.
So I put that to one side, contracts bigger than the rest of my business almost.
And it would be a lovely bonus to have.
But.
And I'm told by the CEO who's English, who loves me, that it's going to happen.
I just need to be patient.
But we're the lead agency, we're the brand that defines the airline in airside and land side, internally, externally, from tail to lounges, uniforms to catering, fragrance to gifting.
We've helped them appoint Gray as the advertising agency and we've been with them shoulder to shoulder going to see Airbus and all sorts of things.
So the whole thing went quite a long way down the line.

And I stupidly, with hindsight, trusted them to a point that I speculated about 60k's worth of hard costs in the last year on them paying at least that by the end of the fiscal year, which they didn't, and 180 grands worth of uncharged commercial time in consulting fees.
So I would have had a materially very different year end to March 25 than I have had.
I would have much better KPIs profitability, net profits, income per head, all sorts of things which I can take you through in a second.
But you know, business is all about speculating.
You don't win everything and sometimes you have to go with your gut and as big as most exciting branding opportunity in 33 years, 32 years to do that.
So I have no regrets.
And we're still in with a fight, so that's kind of where I am.
I'll take a pause for breath there.
Wow, Epic.
So yeah, I mean it's, it's a very established business over a relatively long period of time.
And can I just sort of dig into some of the stuff you've said, just try and understand what the business looks like today?

Because I know you have historically just been a branding business, but you listed out a bunch of other things at the start which included like innovation and experiential and cultural stuff and all that.
So how much of your business today is made up by non brand work.
If I've understood the question?
As simply as you've put it, I would say everything we do is brand related.
So none of it is non brand.
Everything we do has got a brand touch point to it that we end up influencing.
But for example, what I'm not doing is I'm not building websites, but I'm finding people who will.
I'm making films, but we don't do films, we find people who do them for us.

So we're outsourcing kind of marketing mix activation elements which we then either take responsibility to curate and ensure the integrity of the messaging and the image and style and put a markup fee on that for doing that on behalf of the client.
It could be a photo shoot, it could Be a film, it could be an animation.
But I'm not doing, you know, customer relationship stuff.
I'm not doing social, we're not doing influencer, all those type of other marketing mix specific disciplines.
Everything's to do with brand.
I'm just trying to broaden the interpretation of.
Oh, you do consumable, good brand.
Anything that you can eat, drink, put on your skin.
Where now I'm doing more service branding, I'm doing more environmental branding, I'm doing more B2B branding, I'm doing more comms.
Okay.
So the types of clients, it's not, it's not consumer goods as the core type of client.
Obviously the, the airline makes a big change to that as well.
Yeah, we do.
And so you're doing, you said agri and pharma and a bunch of other stuff.
Yeah.
Okay.
But it is mostly brand led.
So if you were to do a brand experience, for instance, you would just make sure it all looked right, but somebody else would do the actual event and.
Correct.
Right, but that would go through you still.
Yeah, a lot of it would.

So in fact today we've taken a brief from Reliance in India who are a big conglomerate group who have asked to test us out on a project to take their successful soft drink brand which they have an identity and guidelines that they don't want to touch.
But they've asked us to imaginatively bring that brand to life around experiences from festivals to retail.

So that's going to take us to working with three dimensional designers who understand set builds, lighting, signage, illumination to create an atmospheric or preferential kind of store and store impact.
And I would work with, you know, a couple of guys who are probably ex future brand or something who run a boutique retail or interior design or experience design.

And I think what, what I'm communicating here Andy, is that we are, we have a brand that has disproportionate value and credibility and sometimes historical equity that people think, oh yeah, they'll get it done.
There's a lot of talent out there who were faceless employees in large big WPP omnicoms or whatever and now they're senior guys or ladies, they're on their own.
They've never run an agency.
They don't know how to do marketing or access clients.
They don't have a brand that attracts the clients.
So they have the capability but they don't have the business.
I have the business, but not necessarily the capability.

So hence this new kind of blue space model that I'm creating which allows me to, instead of Pitching and responding to say, oh, we can't pitch for that because we've got no experience or I don't have the right people in the agency to win that bid.
So I'm not going to bother because I'm limited to what the agency's talent pool is.
I'm now looking at thinking as a businessman, why can't we not do this?
I can find the team and I'll put, in fact, because of this, I'm no longer carrying the cost.
And because of this, it forced me to meet lots of new people and discover great talent out there and build up a bench of people so I can effectively now curate the best team to win it.
And so now it puts many more projects into our potential pipeline than I would have ever considered priority.
Okay.
And that I guess that's just a consequence of the last four years as well, isn't it?
Yeah, it's evolving the offering and just not wanting to carry a big overhead anymore at my age.
I'm not that old.
Okay, cool.
And then you're looking at these different scenarios.
So I guess there's four different scenarios there.
Either stick with growing organically, roll up and I guess if you were running the roll up, you mean where you could acquire a bunch of different agencies, sell, sell to somebody.
I think the roll up, the way you put it is I'm, I, I don't have the liquidity and credit I think to go and borrow a lot of millions from the bank and then go and buy firms.
I also don't think I've got the best financial skills to analyze the health of other companies.

So in the roll up scenario, I was looking at someone like yourself to say, okay, I've got a really progressive digital firm or something or someone who's in America or UK but they'd like to get into India.
You can fast track their ambition growth by them bolting on blue marlin within their mini hub or group.

Or there's two or three firms that complement each other and you're all looking to kind of, you know, monetize your life's work in the next five years, three years, maybe sooner, 18 months, we can put the band together and do a deal for someone, give you critical mass.
Okay, interesting.
Yeah.
So we have some criteria that we are currently putting together for our roll ups that we do.
So there are still fees attached to it, but we do all of the build and put together agencies that are doing 1 million EBITDA.
It's dollars though, so I wouldn't.
Well, you're doing about 340k EBITDA at the moment.
Is that right?
Yeah.
The last year I've just closed, we have our revenues to March were just under 2.3 million.
Our headcount was 17, our staff cost of revenue was 66, our revenue per head was 134.
Our break even per month is about 165.
We made an operating profit of just over 300,000, 13% net.
Yeah, I mean it's, it's not spectacular but it's not a disaster.
Not disaster.
It's a narrow, it is a, I mean it's a profit margin but it's fairly narrow.
Yeah.
And it could be better and it will be better.
Yeah, of course, everyone says that, but circumstantial.
It could be, yeah.
So what I would say is when we're on the buy side we're looking for agencies in the, in the ideal scenario of being somewhere between 23, 20 to 30, sorry, 20 to 30% margin.
Those are like super healthy businesses but Certainly something between 10 and 20 would be on, you know, on somebody's list to acquire.
So I mean it's not terrible but not the best either.
So there definitely must be some savings there.
Are you carrying any staff?
Well, I mean, where's the overhead?
Yeah, I mean I could definitely improve the margin without changing too much of the cost or the revenue.
So for example, you know, I've got a business partner, David, who, who is the lead creative on the Indian work.
He's the legacy co creative founder but he's kind of, between you and I, he's checked out of operational contribution and leadership and drive.
He takes a pro rata 120k salary a year plus benefits, turns up four days a week on, on you know, 1995k and does a basic nine to five.
But you know, in a scenario where I was looking around and looking to save costs, I'd make some revenue savings increases by saving on staff costs and he would be one of the biggest.
But he's a, it's complicated by the fact that he's one of the owners.
He's got, what's he sheld him about.
30, 32, 34% and then you know, again we, you could get into specifics but I think David is two years older than me.
I don't think he's, he's not driven, he's not that ambitious.
He's quite happy to walk away with something as long as it's not insulting and he wants to focus on living rather than working.
So I Think he's primed to be kind of removed, bought out, transitioned out.
You know, I'm, I'm much more involved and I would immodestly say important to the business at the moment, but I'm trying to remove the reliance on Andrew by broadening the leadership team.
I would say so property wise too.
We can reduce our property costs and we're in the process of doing that right now.
Yeah, I mean, if you can get the margin up, then that's really going to help.
Yeah.
At the end of the day, I'm sure you know this, but, but multiples of EBITDA and the profit margin is the way that we get the best valuation for the business.
So I'm sure there's a bunch of other things in there as well.
And usually when we're doing a valuation for a company, we will dig through and see if there's anything that we can take out and make adjustments.
So it may well be that, you know, you've got a car rental or you're putting your petrol through or you.
Oh yeah, there's all of that.
And there's also very generous pension contributions.
You know, we, we've done very well.

So in fact, in the last year, I think we, we hadn't, we'd helped the company out 18 months before by suspending our pension contributions, but we caught up and slugged in another, you know,150,000 into our pensions.
David and mine.
Yeah, you wouldn't, I mean, obviously if you're doing that for valuation reasons versus, you know, just cash flow, I guess.
Yeah, but for valuation reasons you wouldn't have to adjust that.
Those are adjustments that could be made at the time when the transaction, you know, pre transaction.
But when you're, when you're doing the calculation there, that would be when you would say, right, we're excluding all this other stuff that we can just take out.
So.

Yeah, I mean, those adjustments, it's difficult to say just looking at the figure, but obviously if the margin is fairly low and all of that stuff can be added back, you including 120k partner, then that all adds on to the.
Yeah, I mean, I, I, my honesty gut feel would be, I, I am probably, probably with some not too much difficulty, I think we could get to 16 to 18%.
But I, you know, I think we're also subject to this, this withholding tax that we can bring back or not to the business.
Yeah, well, I think that's, it might have to be something we leave on the back burner until the Last minute to see what we, we can get.
But all right, and then just in terms like a valuation.
So most businesses your size, they're going somewhere between sort of three and five times multiple.
So if we just get an average of that and say that currently the business is worth about 2 million pounds, that's kind of like the, the starting point.
Where do you need to exit to be a happy Exeter?
For me personally, I've got about 42% of the business.
My brother has 11.
He doesn't need any money.
He's made, made his and retired as an oil trader in America.
You know, there was a time when I, I would advance that quite bullishly, but I have property, I have pension, I have assets, I have a home.
I would not be unhappy if, if I own half of that number.
And you said, well, the business, we can do a deal at two, two and a half million quid.
I'd be, I'd be okay with that taking 42% of that.
I think I'm at a point where I, I would rather have time then lots of money.
Sounds like you've done really well as well.
So that's good.
Yeah, a lot of people just store it all up in the business and then becomes a real emotional drag.
But you know, realistically, service businesses can only go for so many multiples because it's so easy for a service business to fall apart when the founder steps away.
So.
I mean I, I am asset rich.
I've got a wonderful home with 40 acres of land around it and I've got two commercial buildings which are in my pension fund, one of which I'm selling off now.
So I, I probably have in, in, in bricks and mortar inland.
I have probably about 3, 8 to 5 million in, in, in value and then I have obviously whatever value is left in my business and, and a few other investments.
So I'm not looking for a huge amount of money, but I'm looking for a reasonable amount.
I mean, what I need to weigh up is, is it enough to stop?
Because I love what I do.
You know, I'm earning personally, I'm earning with my, my health, my pension contribution, my salary and all the other perks.
I'm earning about 200 grand a year.
So if someone gives me a million quid, well, I'm going to earn that pre tax, you know, in the next five years.
So it's not going to exactly change my world.
I could just keep working and enjoying trips to India on the back of, you know, business trips.
And things like that.

But it's more about what we're going to do with the business and, and if, if someone can, you know, I'm going to work hard, whatever to make this business more successful and extract more cash out of it in the five years I've got planned, even if I just hand it over.
I've got a daughter who works at WPP as a strategy director.
I've got a design bridge and partners.
I've got another daughter who works at Bain Consulting in Hong Kong.
The two of them would make a killer.
But I'm not forcing my 33 and 31 year old daughters to take over.
As you know, Blue Marlin daughters, generation two.
I think that's, that's a romantic ideal.

So I, I really, I, I, if my job is to run a healthy business and make it as profitable as I can, which I'm going to do, and if this scenario arrives that, that the business is then making 455, 50, 650 profits a year and I step out of it as chairman, help them out few days a month and draw a nice dividend as the owner or a reduced equity partner in my retirement, have an income that's fine too.
You know, it's not like there's a candle or a fire burning under the house.
So I'm just looking to be creative with what might be out there by just at least taking the trouble to talk to someone like you and look at what's possible.
And I just thought the Indian thing is really quite unique.

If there was one thing that you could talk to me about on a plane or in a room and say, right, tell me how many people in this room have got a mature business in India with multinationals at top level, executive contact growing fast, you know, there'd be very few hands up in the room.
I just spoke to a guy yesterday.
But yeah, and I think that's probably the most valuable thing I have to offer.
Yeah, I mean it is fairly unique but funnily enough, yeah, I have just recently spoken to this guy.
Yesterday he was interested in buying something similar to this but not as good as what you're doing and also with no connection to India.
So yeah, let's just go through your options.
I think the main thing is you're staying in for the next five years.
So the initial valuation that I'm giving you, it potentially could be higher than that.
But I think even today with those adjustments made, the valuation of the business around that would be a good exit to have anyway.
So let's look at the other stuff that you've got because those are all available as options today.
So I think if you went to market there would be a lot of interest, particularly the adjustments that you've made to the services that you offer.
So I'll be honest, we tried to sell a brand in company that was really, really good in Yorkshire and we did get a lot of interest, but the multiples that they wanted to exit at were too high.
And I think a lot of offers came between sort of 3 and 4x, which sounds like it's not a massive issue for you.
But the branding space, I think it's quite, I hate to say commoditized, but I think there's a lot of talent out there.
And so the value of an agency that just can do it is not massively high because there's a lot of individuals that can do it as well.
So I guess like you say, people can win the business under almost any brand, let's say, and then hire the talent to deliver it.
If it's part of a bigger job, you know, and part of their other core services, potentially they can do it.

summary.short_summary: Andrew Eyles outlined a potential exit strategy for Blue Marlin, aiming for a sale between ages 65-67, retaining 42% ownership. The company, with a 32-year legacy and total billings of £250 million, currently generates £2.3 million in revenue with a 13% net margin and a team of 17 staff. Notably, operations in India saw a 60% growth to £1.2 million last year, with projections of £1.6 million for this year, despite facing 15% withholding tax challenges that affect financial performance. Blue Marlin secured a $4 million project with Aspire Airlines but faced delays in funding due to tariff issues. The business is valued at £2-2.5 million based on a 3-5x EBITDA multiple and is considering mergers with complementary agencies to enhance market position and increase valuation multiples.
